newsitem.title: USA: Tyson lobbyist pleads not guilty in Espy probe.
newsitem.headline: Tyson lobbyist pleads not guilty in Espy probe.

text.p: Tyson Foods lobbyist Jack Williams pleaded not guilty on Friday to charges that he lied to government investigators looking into the conduct of former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy.

Williams is now set to go to trial in the U.S. District Court here in December, and could face stiff fines and up to ten years in prison if convicted of two criminal counts returned against him earlier this month.

Williams, who represented the interests of the giant Arkansas-based poultry processor in Washington and elsewhere, was charged with knowingly making false statements to the FBI and the Agriculture Department's Office of Inspector General during preliminary scrutiny of Espy in early 1994.

The alleged crime took place before Independent Counsel Donald Smaltz was named to head a special investigation of the former Clinton cabinet member. Espy resigned as head of the huge agriculture agency in 1994 amid accusations that he had illegally accepted gifts and favors from companies his agency was in charge of regulating, including Tyson Foods.

Tyson Foods, the nation's biggest chicken processor with annual sales of over $5 billion and long close ties to President Clinton, allegedly wined and dined Espy and his girlfriend in 1993 and 1994 with gifts that included tickets and limousine transportation to a National Football League playoff game in Dallas, as well as giving the girlfriend an educational scholarship worth $1,200 per semester.

According to the Smaltz investigation team, Williams was key in arranging with Tyson's corporate office the details of the football game transportation and other services to Espy and his friend, paid for the girlfriend's airplane ticket to Dallas, and helped coordinate the scholarship.
Upon questioning by investigators, however, Williams denied that he knew anything about the gifts and favors, or had any role in the alleged activities.

The government's two-year investigation of Espy received a shot in the arm earlier this week when a federal jury convicted the giant fruit cooperative Sun-Diamond of California on eight criminal counts that included giving illegal gratuities to Espy and illegal campaign contributions to Espy's brother, Henry.
Legal experts said the verdict was significant in that it lent credibility to the widespread probe and provided a important psychological boost to the investigators.
Experts said it also did not bode well for other pending cases in the investigation and could persuade reluctant witnesses to now cooperate with the government.
Tyson Foods is still being investigated by Smaltz and his team, and sources close to the case have said that an indictment of the company or its senior officials cannot be ruled out.
